1.q: וּ⁠בְנֵ֨י רְאוּבֵ֥ן בְּכֽוֹר־יִשְׂרָאֵל֮ כִּ֣י ה֣וּא הַ⁠בְּכוֹר֒ וּֽ⁠בְ⁠חַלְּל⁠וֹ֙ יְצוּעֵ֣י אָבִ֔י⁠ו נִתְּנָה֙ בְּכֹ֣רָת֔⁠וֹ לִ⁠בְנֵ֥י יוֹסֵ֖ף בֶּן־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְ⁠לֹ֥א לְ⁠הִתְיַחֵ֖שׂ לַ⁠בְּכֹרָֽה כִּ֤י יְהוּדָה֙ גָּבַ֣ר בְּ⁠אֶחָ֔י⁠ו וּ⁠לְ⁠נָגִ֖יד מִמֶּ֑⁠נּוּ וְ⁠הַ⁠בְּכֹרָ֖ה לְ⁠יוֹסֵֽף
1.note: Before listing the descendants of Reuben, the author provides background information to explain why he has not listed them first, given that Reuben was the oldest son of Israel. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine [5:1](ta:05) and 5:2 into a verse bridge in order provide this background information before the introduction of the list of Reuben’s descendants. Alternate translation: [The tribe of Judah became the largest tribe, and the first great king of Israel came from that tribe, so this genealogy has listed the descendants of Judah first. Reuben was the oldest son of Israel, and ordinarily the family of the oldest son would be listed first. But because Reuben had sexual relations with one of his father’s secondary wives, his father gave the rights of the oldest son to the sons of his brother Joseph. (Judah was not listed first on the basis of those rights, since they belonged to Joseph.) So here now is a list of Reuben’s descendants]

Here, **the couches** of Reuben’s **father** represent with wives with whom he would have sexual relations on a couch or bed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [but when he defiled his father’s marriage bed] or [but when he had unlawful sexual relations with one of the wives of his father]

The expression **was given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [his father gave his birthright]

In many cultures, it may not seem to be possible for a father to give the rights of a firstborn son to the **sons** of his **son**, that is, to his grandsons. The explanation is that Israel (Jacob) had adopted Ephraim and Manasseh, the first two sons of **Joseph**, as his own sons, as Genesis 48:5 describes. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to the two sons of his son Joseph whom he had adopted]

The expression **is not enrolled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [so this genealogy does not list him]

2.note: Here, **Judah** represents the tribe of Judah, and **his brothers** represent the other Israelite tribes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the tribe of Judah became the largest of all the tribes of Israel]

Here, **Joseph** represents his two sons Ephraim and Manasseh, as the previous verse indicates. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph]

6.note: The author is spelling this foreign name the way Hebrew speakers of his place and time would have said it. At an earlier time, they said it slightly differently as “Tiglath Pileser,” as 2 Kings 15:29 and 2 Kings 16:7 show. Recall whether your translation team decided to use the same name for a given person in each place where he appears or whether you decided to use the name that the biblical author does, even if that is a variant. Alternate translation: [Tiglath Pileser]

The author is not referring to a specific **Reubenite**. He means the Reubenites, the descendants of Reuben, in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [of the Reubenites]

7.note: The pronoun **his** could refer back to: (1) Beerah, in verse 6. Alternate translation: [And Beerah’s brothers] or (2) Joel, in verse 4. Alternate translation: [And Joel’s brothers]

The author is speaking as if the men he lists were actual **brothers** of Beerah. He is using the term to describe people who are descended from the same ancestor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and in similar contexts throughout the book. Alternate translation: [And his kinsmen] or [And his relatives]

The four men listed in verses 6–8 (Beerah, Jeiel, Zechariah, and Bela) seem to be leaders of the four clans of the tribe of Reuben listed in verse 3. The pronoun **his** may therefore refer to Reuben. However, it could also refer to each of these leaders individually, and it may be more natural in your language to use a plural pronoun. Alternate translation: [in the clans of Reuben] or [in their clans]

The author is using the image of the **head** to mean a leader. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and in comparable contexts in the rest of the book. Alternate translation: [the leader] or [a clan leader]

The expression **being enrolled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [as their genealogies record them]

10.note: The author is using the term **days** to refer to a specific time, the time when Saul was the king of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And during the reign of Saul]
The author is using the term **fell** to mean that the Hagrites died, since soldiers fall down when they die in battle. Alternate translation: [and they died]

The author is using the term **hand** to represent power. See the discussion of this usage in the introduction to 1 Chronicles. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [at the hands of the Reubenites] or [because the Reubenites were stronger]

Here, the **tents** of the Hagrites represent the territory on which they lived in those tents. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And they occupied their territory]

The author is speaking as if the surface of the ground or the habitable land in the region of Gilead were actually its **face**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the land in the eastern part of the region of Gilead]

11.note: The author is speaking as if the people of the tribe of Gad were actually the **sons** of Gad. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Gad]

16.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:23. Alternate translation: [and in the surrounding villages]

17.note: The expression **were enrolled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Officials enrolled all of them]

17.q: בִּ⁠ימֵ֖י יוֹתָ֣ם מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֑ה וּ⁠בִ⁠ימֵ֖י יָרָבְעָ֥ם מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
17.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 4:41. Alternate translation: [during the reign of Jothan as king of Judah and during the reign of Jeroboam as king of Israel]

18.note: The author is not referring to a specific **Gadite**. He means the Gadites (the members of the tribe of Gad) in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the Gadites]

In certain contexts, biblical authors and characters use the expression **son of** to indicate that a person has the characteristic of something. In this case, these **men** were characterized by their **valor** or courage and prowess in warfare. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [valiant warriors]

The author is not referring to a specific **shield** or **sword**. He means those weapons in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [men who carried shields and swords] or [men armed with shields and swords]

Ancient archers would step or tread on their bows in order to bend them so that they could string them. The author is using this action to represent the entire use of a bow in battle, especially shooting arrows at enemy soldiers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and who were skillful archers]

The expression **taught** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. The UST models one way to do that.

19.note: The author is using the names of these cities to represent the people who lived in them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the inhabitants of Jetur and Naphish and Nodab]

20.q: וַ⁠יֵּעָזְר֣וּ עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֔ם וַ⁠יִּנָּתְנ֤וּ בְ⁠יָדָ⁠ם֙ הַֽ⁠הַגְרִיאִ֔ים וְ⁠כֹ֖ל שֶׁ֣⁠עִמָּ⁠הֶ֑ם כִּ֠י לֵ⁠אלֹהִ֤ים זָעֲקוּ֙ בַּ⁠מִּלְחָמָ֔ה וְ⁠נַעְתּ֥וֹר לָ⁠הֶ֖ם כִּי־ בָ֥טְחוּ בֽ⁠וֹ
20.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could change the order of these phrases in order to put the reasons before the results. Alternate translation: [They cried out to God in the battle, and since they trusted in him, he was entreated by them, and so they were helped against them, and the Hagrites and all who {were} with them were given into their hand]

20.q: וַ⁠יֵּעָזְר֣וּ עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֔ם וַ⁠יִּנָּתְנ֤וּ בְ⁠יָדָ⁠ם֙ הַֽ⁠הַגְרִיאִ֔ים וְ⁠כֹ֖ל שֶׁ֣⁠עִמָּ⁠הֶ֑ם
20.note: The expressions **were helped** and **were given** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active forms or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And God helped them to fight them, and he gave the Hagrites and all who were with them into their hand]

Here, **hand** represents “power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he gave the Hagrites and all who were with them into their power] or [and he enabled them to defeat the Hagrites and their allies]

The expression **was entreated** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and they successfully entreated him]

21.note: The author is not referring to a specific **soul** of a particular **man**. He means the souls of all 100,000 men whom the Israelites captured. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and souls of men]
The author is using one part of a person, his **soul**, to mean all of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and human beings]

22.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [The Israelites won the battle because]

22.q: חֲלָלִ֤ים רַבִּים֙ נָפָ֔לוּ כִּ֥י מֵ⁠הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֖ים הַ⁠מִּלְחָמָ֑ה
22.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [since the battle was from God, many fell slain]

The author is using ** the battle {was} from God** as a common expression of his culture to mean that God was helping the Israelites win the battle. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God was helping the Israelites win the battle]

23.note: The author is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they multiplied** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to indicate that it was specifically the people of **half of the tribe of Manasseh**, rather than all of the Israelites he describes in verse 18, who **multiplied** in the territories they all conquered. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [For their part, they multiplied]

24.note: See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of how the author uses the term **heads** to mean “leaders” and the expression **house of their fathers** to mean “their extended families” or “their clans.” Alternate translation: [And these were leaders of their clans]

The author is using the term **names** to represent the reputations that these men won as great **warriors**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [men with great reputations]

25.note: The author is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their ancestors]

When the author says that these Israelites **whored after** foreign gods, he is using that to represent how they were unfaithful to Yahweh by worshiping other gods, just as a wife would be unfaithful to her husband by being with other men. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they were unfaithful to him by worshiping]

The author is using **from their faces** as a common expression of his culture to mean “on account of them” or “for their sake.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for their sake] or [so that they could live in the land]

26.q: וַ⁠יָּעַר֩ אֱלֹהֵ֨י יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל אֶת־ ר֣וּחַ ׀ פּ֣וּל מֶֽלֶךְ־ אַשּׁ֗וּר וְ⁠אֶת־ ר֨וּחַ֙ תִּלְּגַ֤ת פִּלְנֶ֨סֶר֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר
26.note: The author is speaking as if the **spirit** of each of these kings had actually been asleep and God **awakened** it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [So the God of Israel influenced Pul, the king of Assyria, and Tilgath Pilneser, the king of Assyria, to want to conquer them]
See how you decided to spell this name in 5:6. Alternate translation: [Tiglath Pileser]

The author is not referring to a specific **Reubenite** or **Gadite**. He means the members of those tribes in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Reubenites and the Gadites]
See the discussion of the phrase **to this day** in the introduction to 1 Chronicles. Alternate translation: [and they have remained there permanently]
